lead: The Internet is not one network but millions of networks joined by one common set of rules: the TCP/IP protocol suite. It sorts every networking job into four layers — application, transport, internet, network access — and hands data down from one to the next. IP sits in the middle as the narrow waist: one packet format that every link below and every service above must fit through. The architecture is an edge of hosts and access links joined to a core of routers run by competing ISPs. Every UPI payment, video call and email rides this stack.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.5 for the seven OSI layers, and Chapter 1.4 for what a layer, a header and a peer are.

blocks.text: TCP/IP is the protocol suite the Internet really runs on. It groups all networking jobs into four layers. Each layer takes data from the layer above, adds its own header, and passes the result down. The figure shows the stack with the main protocols in each layer.

items: Application: HTTP, DNS, SMTP, FTP, DHCP. Serves the user's program directly.
Transport: TCP, UDP. Cuts data into segments and delivers each to the right program on the right host.
Internet: IP, ICMP, ARP. Moves a packet from any host to any host across many networks.
Network access: Ethernet, Wi-Fi, PPP. Wraps the packet in a frame and then in bits on one link.

blocks.text: The bottom layer carries two jobs at once: the data link job and the physical job. Many Indian textbooks split it and teach five layers — application, transport, network, data link, physical. Both lists describe the same stack. If a question says five-layer model, split the bottom block; if it says four, keep it whole.

The application and transport layers run only in the two end hosts. The internet layer runs in the hosts and in every router along the path. The network access layer runs on the hosts and on every device of the link, including switches and access points.
IP's contract is short: connectionless, best-effort, unreliable, with no order guarantee.

items: Connectionless: no setup before sending. The packet is handed to the network and forgotten.
Best-effort: the network tries, and promises nothing more. A congested router may drop the packet.
Unreliable: a dropped, duplicated or corrupted packet is not reported back to the sender.
No order guarantee: packet 2 may arrive before packet 1.

blocks.text: Every packet carries a destination IP address and is forwarded one hop at a time. Each router decides alone, from its own routing table, which link to use next. Two packets of the same file can take different routes and arrive out of order.

Why accept so little? A simple service is cheap to build and works over any link — fibre, Wi-Fi, satellite. IP is the narrow waist: everything above and everything below must fit through one packet format. If you need reliability, TCP adds it above IP; if you do not, UDP skips it. The repair happens at the endpoints, never inside the routers.

The Internet's architecture has two parts. The edge is the end systems — phones, laptops, servers — plus the access networks that connect them. The core is the mesh of routers and long links that carries packets between ISPs.

items: Access networks: home fibre or DSL with Wi-Fi, mobile 4G/5G, campus Ethernet, a café hotspot.
ISP tiers: a local ISP buys transit from a regional ISP, which buys from a tier-1 backbone.
Internet exchange point (IXP): a building where many ISPs swap traffic directly instead of paying transit.
Content providers: large ones run their own backbone and place caches close to users.

blocks.text: Route of one packet: your phone → Wi-Fi access point → home router, your default gateway → the ISP's first router → more routers → maybe an IXP → the destination's ISP → the destination host. At each router the incoming link header is stripped, the IP destination is read, the routing table is searched, and a fresh link header is added for the next hop. The IP address stays the same end to end; the link address changes at every hop.
Nothing forces all packets of a flow onto one path, so one packet can overtake another. Addressing and routing are in Unit 4; frames and the link layer are in Unit 3.

sections.h3: OSI to TCP/IP, and why jobs sit at the ends

blocks.text: OSI is a reference model; TCP/IP is a working suite. The mapping above is the one examiners expect. Session and presentation jobs are done inside application protocols when they are needed at all.

The end-to-end argument says: put a function in the end hosts unless the network can do it completely and correctly by itself. Reliability is the standard example. A router cannot tell whether a packet was lost or the application stopped caring, so routers only forward. TCP at the two ends checks, retransmits and reorders. The core stays fast and simple; the intelligence sits at the edge.

examples.question: A packet capture lists twelve protocols: HTTP, DNS, SMTP, FTP, DHCP, TCP, UDP, IP, ICMP, ARP, Ethernet, Wi-Fi. Place each in its TCP/IP layer. Then count (a) the protocols in each layer, (b) how many work end to end, (c) how many work hop by hop, and (d) how many sit on the boundary between the internet and network access layers.
steps: Application layer: HTTP, DNS, SMTP, FTP, DHCP. Count = 5.
Internet layer: IP, ICMP, ARP. Count = 3.
Network access layer: Ethernet, Wi-Fi. Count = 2.
Check the total: 5 + 2 + 3 + 2 = 12, which matches the list.
End-to-end means the protocol runs only in the two end hosts: the 5 application protocols + TCP + UDP = 7.
Hop-by-hop means the protocol is processed at every device on the path: IP, ICMP, Ethernet, Wi-Fi = 4.
Boundary: ARP alone = 1. It carries IP addresses inside link frames and stops at the local link.
examples.answer: Application 5, transport 2, internet 3, network access 2; 7 protocols work end to end, 4 work hop by hop, and ARP alone sits on the boundary.
examples.check:
protos = [
    ("HTTP", "application", "end"),
    ("DNS", "application", "end"),
    ("SMTP", "application", "end"),
    ("FTP", "application", "end"),
    ("DHCP", "application", "end"),
    ("TCP", "transport", "end"),
    ("UDP", "transport", "end"),
    ("IP", "internet", "hop"),
    ("ICMP", "internet", "hop"),
    ("ARP", "internet", "boundary"),
    ("Ethernet", "network access", "hop"),
    ("Wi-Fi", "network access", "hop"),
]
for lay in ["application", "transport", "internet", "network access"]:
    print(sum(1 for p, l, s in protos if l == lay))
print(sum(1 for p, l, s in protos if s == "end"))
print(sum(1 for p, l, s in protos if s == "hop"))
print(sum(1 for p, l, s in protos if s == "boundary"))

traps: Drawing seven boxes and calling them TCP/IP. The suite has four layers; the seven-layer model is OSI.
Writing that the network access layer means the data link layer. It covers the physical layer too; the five-layer version is the one that splits them.
Saying IP is reliable because TCP is. IP itself drops, duplicates and reorders; TCP at the ends repairs that, and UDP does not.
Putting ARP fully in the network access layer or fully in the internet layer. It carries IP addresses inside link frames, so it sits on the boundary.
Calling the transport layer 'the reliable layer'. UDP is a transport protocol and gives no reliability at all.
Saying the top three layers run only on the end hosts. The internet layer runs in every router too, because each router reads and rewrites the IP header.

quiz.q: Name the four TCP/IP layers from top to bottom.
Which TCP/IP layer holds HTTP, DNS and SMTP?
What does best-effort mean for IP?
quiz.a: The network makes a reasonable attempt to deliver each packet and guarantees nothing. Packets may be dropped, duplicated, corrupted or delivered out of order, and no error is reported to the sender.

quiz.q: Why do some textbooks show five layers instead of four?
quiz.a: They split the network access layer into a data link layer and a physical layer, as OSI does. The protocols, the order and the jobs do not change; only the bottom block is divided.

quiz.q: Place Ethernet, IP, UDP and SMTP in their TCP/IP layers, from bottom to top.
quiz.a: Ethernet — network access; IP — internet; UDP — transport; SMTP — application.

quiz.q: A phone on Wi-Fi sends a request to a web server in another city. List the devices and networks the packet passes, and say what changes at each hop.
quiz.a: Phone → Wi-Fi access point → home router (default gateway) → ISP access router → regional and backbone routers → possibly an IXP → the server's ISP → the server. The IP address stays the same end to end; the link-layer address is stripped and rewritten at every hop.

quiz.q: A router is modified to check every packet for errors and to ask for retransmission. Use the end-to-end argument to explain why this is a bad design.
quiz.a: The router cannot tell whether a packet was lost or the receiver stopped caring, so it would hold state for flows it does not own and duplicate a job TCP already does at the ends. Overhead grows in the core, which must stay simple and fast to carry everyone's traffic.

quiz.q: Why is ARP said to sit on the boundary between the internet and network access layers?
quiz.a: ARP asks 'which link address owns this IP address?'. It uses an IP address, an internet-layer identifier, but the question and the answer travel inside link-layer frames and never leave the local link. It needs both layers and fits cleanly in neither.

beyond: Not for the exam. The narrow waist is still IP, but new work leans on it: QUIC runs above UDP, in user space, and builds its own reliability and encryption there, so HTTP/3 gets TCP-like delivery without TCP. Large content providers also push caches deep into access ISPs. Firewalls and NAT boxes now sit in the middle of many paths, so researchers still argue about how far the end-to-end argument holds. Search 'narrow waist', 'QUIC', 'Internet exchange point' and 'end-to-end argument' to go further.
